metaDescription: Six portable emergency lights compared, from pocket-sized lanterns to rechargeable power bank lights, for carrying light wherever the outage finds you.
introParagraphs: A portable emergency light earns its place by going where you go. Plug-in lights and bulbs stay put, but an outage rarely cooperates: you need light in the kitchen, then the basement, then the porch to check a breaker or a fuse. A good portable light can be carried, hung from a hook or set on a table, and it works in any room without needing a free outlet or a lamp.

The six lights here fall into two groups. The Lepro 4 Pack, the MalloMe lantern and the Etekcity 2 Pack are small, collapsible, battery-powered lanterns that tuck into a drawer. The Glocusent, the Eventek and the CAVN are larger rechargeable lights with big batteries; the Eventek and the Glocusent also work as power banks, and the CAVN adds a remote control and a telescopic stand. Each group answers a different question: how small can it be, and how long can it run.

We evaluated every pick from its listing specs and typical buyer feedback, and brightness and runtime figures are the makers' claims. The goal is a short list that suits an active adult, which means light weight, clear controls and sensible storage.

products.name: Glocusent LED Rechargeable Camping Lantern

specList.label: Runtime
specList.value: Up to 200 hours on low (maker claim)

products.description:
The Glocusent is the best all-around portable light here because it balances brightness, runtime and ease of use. It has 135 LEDs that produce an even 360 degree glow, a 5000mAh rechargeable battery, three color temperatures and five brightness levels. The listing claims up to 200 hours on the lowest setting and about 12 hours at the highest.

That range makes it flexible. Low and warm is a comfortable evening glow for a living room, and the bright cool setting is good for finding something in a closet. The color modes mean you do not have to accept a harsh white light at midnight. The trade-off is that it is a lantern you charge by cable, so it needs a schedule, and it does not come on by itself.

Compared with the Lepro 4 Pack, which uses disposable batteries, the Glocusent saves money over time and carries far more battery capacity. It is larger and heavier than the pocket lanterns, so keep it on a shelf where you can lift it easily. For most people, one Glocusent plus a few small lanterns is the best-balanced set. Treat it as the lantern that stays in the family room, and recharge it whenever you notice the indicator dropping. Because the lowest mode is so frugal, you can leave it glowing as a night light through a long evening without worrying.
products.bestFor: One versatile lantern that handles both an evening outage and a quick search.
pros: Up to 200 hours on low by the maker's claim

products.name: Eventek 20000mAh Rechargeable LED Work Light
products.description:
The Eventek is the strongest option for anyone who worries about phones as well as light. Its 20000mAh lithium polymer battery is the largest here, with a claimed 144 hours of runtime and dual USB-A outputs for charging devices. The listing describes 40 high-brightness LEDs at 12W, an infinitely dimmable output and a rotatable head.

In an outage, that makes the Eventek both a lamp and a charging station. You can keep a phone alive while you read the lights, which is a real comfort for people who rely on their phone for news and calls. It is also the heaviest of the group, so it is better placed on a table than carried everywhere.

Compared with the Glocusent, the Eventek offers more battery capacity and the infinite dimming dial, but it gives up the extra color modes. If you worry about long outages, this is the one to keep charged on a shelf. Check it monthly and top it up, since a big battery that sits empty helps no one. A sensible routine is to top it up on the first day of each season and leave the cable next to it. Pair it with a Lepro lantern in the bedroom so the heavy light never has to climb the stairs.
products.bestFor: People who want light and phone charging from one device during a long outage.

products.name: Lepro LED Camping Lanterns, 4 Pack
products.description:
The Lepro 4 Pack is the lightweight answer. Each lantern weighs 55 grams with batteries, is smaller than a standard A19 bulb, and includes a hanging hook. The listing describes three modes: a low beam at 80 lumens in either daylight white or soft white, lasting about 10 hours, and a high beam at 140 lumens.

The tiny size is a real benefit for pockets, glove compartments, and bags. A set of four means a lantern can live in every room, the car and a purse. The downside is limited brightness, so it will not flood a large room, and it uses disposable batteries that must be replaced.

Compared with the Glocusent, the Lepro is lighter and cheaper to scatter around the house, but it cannot match the Glocusent for runtime. Treat it as the grab-and-go layer in a mixed setup. It is also an easy gift for a family member who wants a light in the car and by the bed. Hang one on a closet rod, one on the garage door handle and one on the car visor, and you will always find a light close by. Remember to replace the cells together so all four lanterns stay equally ready.
products.bestFor: Scattering several small lights around the house, car and bags.

products.name: MalloMe Camping LED Lantern
products.description:
The MalloMe is the lantern with the simplest control: you pull it up to light it and push it down to turn it off. The listing describes advanced COB LED technology giving up to 300 lumens of even light, and a build that is durable, water resistant and lightweight. Foldaway handles let you carry or hang it.

Because there is no button to find in the dark, it suits anyone who prefers a mechanical action. It is also the brightest of the compact lanterns here, beating the Etekcity at 154 lumens and the Lepro at 140 lumens. The limitation is the lack of a dimming mode in the listing, so it is either on or off.

It is sold as a single lantern, so buy a few if you want to place them in different rooms. Keep spare batteries in the same drawer. For someone who values simplicity and a strong beam, the MalloMe is a thoughtful, no-fuss choice. Because it needs no menu, it is the lantern you would happily hand to a houseguest without explaining anything. Store it collapsed on a shelf near the door so it is the first thing you reach for.
products.bestFor: Quick, mechanical operation with a strong beam from a compact body.
pros: Turns on by pulling it up

products.name: CAVN Rechargeable Camping Lights with Remote
products.description:
The CAVN is the most feature-rich light here. It offers five lighting modes including warm, white and spotlight, a 10000mAh rechargeable battery with a USB output, a remote control, and a detachable telescopic tripod that extends from about 30 inches to about 72 inches. At a stated 2200 lumens, it is also very bright.

The tripod lets you set the light high to flood a room from above, which is helpful for a garage, a workshop or a porch. The remote means you can switch modes without getting up. That feature set also means more to learn, and the tripod adds bulk when stored.

Compared with the Eventek, the CAVN is brighter and more adjustable but has half the battery capacity. It is a good choice for people who want a standing floor light during a long outage, but it is not the lantern to toss in a drawer. If you buy it, set it up once on a sunny afternoon so you know how the remote pairs and how the tripod locks. A half-learned tool is hard to use well in the dark and in a hurry.
products.bestFor: A standing floodlight for workspaces and large rooms.

products.name: Etekcity LED Camping Lanterns, 2 Pack
products.description:
The Etekcity pair is a sensible everyday lantern set. Each lantern has 30 LEDs reaching 154 lumens with a 360 degree spread, collapses to roughly the size of a phone and dims by how far you extend it. They suit a bedroom and a kitchen.

The lanterns are easy to understand and easy to store. They are less bright than the MalloMe at 300 lumens, but comfortable for reading and finding things. The listing does not state a runtime, so we do not repeat one.

As a pair, they sit between single lanterns and the larger four-packs. Choose them if you want two matching lights without the commitment of a big set. They are a good starter set for a couple. The pair also makes a tidy gift, because the two lanterns are identical and easy to explain. Place one by the bed and one in the kitchen, and the main evening routine is covered.
products.bestFor: A matching pair for the bedroom and kitchen.
cons: No runtime figure in the listing

buyingCriteria.explanation: A portable light is only useful if you can carry it comfortably. The Lepro weighs 55g with batteries, while the Eventek and CAVN with their large batteries are much heavier. Look for a handle or hook you can hold securely. Test the weight with your usual carry hand before you buy. Make this check before the storm season rather than during it, because stores run short of batteries and cables when a forecast turns bad.

Battery capacity is shown in mAh. The Eventek has 20000mAh, the CAVN has 10000mAh and the Glocusent has 5000mAh, while the Lepro uses small disposable cells. Bigger batteries last longer and can charge phones, but they weigh more. Choose capacity to match how long outages run in your area. Make this check before the storm season rather than during it, because stores run short of batteries and cables when a forecast turns bad.

Output ranges from 140 lumens on the Lepro to 2200 lumens on the CAVN. About 80 lumens lights a room, so most indoor needs are modest. Warm modes, like the Glocusent offers, are gentler at night. Pick a light with a low mode for overnight. Make this check before the storm season rather than during it, because stores run short of batteries and cables when a forecast turns bad.

Some lights double as chargers. The Eventek has dual USB-A outputs, the CAVN has a USB output and the Glocusent is described as a power bank. During an outage, a phone is a lifeline for news and calls. Remember that charging a phone shortens lighting time. Make this check before the storm season rather than during it, because stores run short of batteries and cables when a forecast turns bad.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Controls you can use in the dark
buyingCriteria.explanation: Simple controls matter most when the lights are out. The MalloMe turns on by pulling it up, the Etekcity dims by height, and the CAVN uses a remote. Try the control with your eyes closed to see if it is intuitive. Avoid lights with many press-and-hold combinations. Make this check before the storm season rather than during it, because stores run short of batteries and cables when a forecast turns bad.

A rechargeable light needs a top-up every few months. Disposable-battery lanterns like the Lepro and MalloMe need spare cells. Store lights where you can find them in the dark and write the charge date on a tag. A light that lives in a dead drawer is no help. Make this check before the storm season rather than during it, because stores run short of batteries and cables when a forecast turns bad.

howWeEvaluated.title: Portability
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared weight, size and carrying features. The Lepro at 55g with batteries is the lightest, while the Eventek and CAVN are heavier. Handles and hooks earned points.

howWeEvaluated.title: Battery and runtime
howWeEvaluated.description: We read capacities and runtime claims from each listing. The Eventek leads with 20000mAh and up to 144 hours, the Glocusent claims up to 200 hours on low, and the CAVN has 10000mAh. All figures are maker claims.

howWeEvaluated.title: Brightness range
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated output and modes, from the Lepro at 140 lumens to the CAVN at 2200 lumens. Lights with both low and high settings scored best.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ease of control
howWeEvaluated.description: We favored simple operation. The MalloMe pull-up design and Etekcity height dimming led here, while the CAVN's remote added flexibility.

howWeEvaluated.title: Added functions
howWeEvaluated.description: We noted extras such as power bank outputs, a tripod and hooks. The Eventek and CAVN lead on extras, but extras only count when they are useful.

howToChoose.note: Keep one light in the car as well.
A mix of one big and several small lights is a smart plan.

howToChoose.intro: Power source is the main trade-off.

cards.label: Disposable batteries
cards.text: The Lepro 4 Pack, MalloMe and Etekcity use replaceable cells. They are light, fast to refresh and work with a spare set, but need a supply of batteries.

cards.label: Rechargeable
cards.text: The Glocusent, Eventek and CAVN hold large built-in batteries and double as chargers. They cost less to run but need a charging routine. Choose disposable for grab-and-go and rechargeable for long outages.

howToChoose.note: Avoid very bright lights in small bedrooms.

howToChoose.intro: Several days without power is the hard case.

cards.text: Look for a big battery, a low mode and a way to charge phones. Efficiency matters more than peak brightness.

faq.q: What makes a light portable for emergencies?
faq.a: It should be light enough to carry, have a handle or hook, and work without an outlet. Collapsible lanterns like the Lepro and MalloMe meet that. Larger lights like the Eventek are portable but heavier. Look for a handle you can grip with one hand. A lantern with a ring or hook can also hang from a doorknob or cabinet handle, which frees both hands during a blackout.

faq.q: Which is better, rechargeable or battery operated?
faq.a: Rechargeable lights like the Glocusent save on batteries but need charging. Battery lights like the Lepro are ready with spare cells. Many households keep one of each for flexibility. It is worth owning at least one of each type. Check the listing for how each model charges, because a light that takes a wall adapter you cannot find in the dark is little help.

The Eventek has dual USB outputs and the Glocusent is described as a power bank. The CAVN also has a USB output. Charging a phone reduces light runtime. Keep a short cable in the same drawer as the light. If a power bank function matters to you, top up the phone first and keep the light on its lowest setting to stretch the runtime.

faq.q: How bright should a portable light be?
faq.a: Around 80 lumens lights a small room, and 150 to 300 lumens suits most indoor tasks. Very bright lights like the CAVN at 2200 lumens are best for large or outdoor spaces. Pick the dimmest mode that still lets you see comfortably. For hallways and stairs, a steady mid mode is usually easier on the eyes than a maximum setting that creates glare on walls.

Keep lights in a known spot such as a hall closet or kitchen drawer, with spare batteries nearby. Recharge rechargeable lights every few months. Remove disposable cells if you will not use the light for a year. Label the drawer so others in the home can find them. Writing the month of the last charge on a strip of tape stuck to each light makes the next top up easy to schedule.

Most are low-voltage and safe for ordinary use, but small parts like batteries need care. Keep spare cells out of reach. Strobe modes should not be used around anyone sensitive to flashing light. If in doubt, ask a grown-up to check the lights first. Teach everyone in the house where the lights live and how the switch works, so nobody has to fumble for instructions during an outage.
